issues.title: The Tech Policy Brief, September 2026
issues.summary: AI agents under pressure, warrantless license-plate tracking, three states’ approaches to personalized pricing, and AI’s effect on the economics of journalism, plus an especially long list of fellowships and jobs.

issues.html:
The Tech Policy Hub is collaborating with Phronesis to provide a monthly briefing on developments at the intersection of technology, law, and policy. Focused on signal over noise.

Can you believe how fast the year is flying by? We sure can’t!

First, let’s address the elephant in the room: yes, our September newsletter is arriving a little later than usual. To make up for it, we’ve packed this issue with plenty of opportunities and some exciting news we can’t wait to share.

So, without further ado, let’s get into it!

1. From Tech Policy Hub & Phronesis

  • A new home for the Tech Policy Hub. Our new website is up and running! You can explore it here.
  • A fresh look for Phronesis. We’ve redesigned the site to better reflect its role as a library and archive of our reading and research at the intersection of technology, law, and policy. Take a look here.
  • Our latest FTC public comment. Members of our team recently submitted another public comment to the Federal Trade Commission, this time on personalized pricing.
  • Join our speaker series. We’re excited to bring you the Tech Policy Hub’s speaker series, with virtual attendance available. Explore the upcoming events here.
  • Research on the move. Our Location Technology and the U.S. Fourth Amendment project has been accepted to EAAMO 2026, and we’re preparing a submission to FAccT. You can read about the accepted project here.
  • Growing the AI Opportunity Inventory. We’re working with the UT Austin School of Law to help expand the AI Opportunity Inventory. Learn more about the initiative here.

2. Signals

AI agents: performance, pressure, and permission

  • More agents do not always mean better results. Research covered by Tech Xplore finds that adding agents can improve some tasks while undermining others. Collaboration helped with financial analysis, but coordination costs reduced performance on sequential planning tasks. The practical takeaway: organizations should test whether delegation improves a particular workflow before assuming that a larger team of agents will perform better.
  • Can enterprise assistants follow rules under pressure? The PACT preprint evaluates 22 models across simulated workplace scenarios and reports that ordinary user pressure increased rule violations by 65% on average. These benchmark findings raise an important deployment question: do safeguards hold when users insist, deadlines loom, or shortcuts become attractive?
  • Whose permission counts when an agent acts? In Amazon v. Perplexity, the Ninth Circuit vacated a preliminary injunction restricting Perplexity’s shopping assistant. On the facts before it, the court treated the user as accessing Amazon through an AI tool. The decision highlights a consequential tension between users’ ability to delegate online tasks and platforms’ control over access, without settling AI-agent liability more broadly.

Surveillance and the Fourth Amendment

  • When does tracking public movement become a search? An early October update: United States v. Brownlee brought warrantless police use of Flock license-plate cameras before the Fifth Circuit. The case raises questions about constitutional protections when camera networks make people’s movements searchable. Listen to the oral argument for the competing positions; the argument itself is not a ruling.

States take different approaches to personalized pricing

  • New York: disclosure and discrimination. S7033 proposed disclosure requirements alongside restrictions on location-based price differences and the use of protected-class data. This particular bill did not become law; its enacting clause was stricken in April. It remains a useful example of the policy choices under consideration.
  • Maryland: restrictions focused on food retail. HB0895, enacted in April with an October 1 effective date, restricts personalized pricing practices by food retailers and third-party delivery providers. Its sector-specific approach illustrates how lawmakers can target particular markets rather than apply one rule across the economy.
  • Connecticut: prohibitions and disclosures. HB05563, now Public Act 26-130, prohibits surveillance pricing by covered retailers and delivery services, subject to exceptions, while requiring disclosures for certain other businesses using it online. The pricing provisions take effect July 1, 2027. Exceptions for discounts and justified price differences make the boundaries of the law especially important.

AI and the economics of journalism

  • Fair use meets concerns about substitution. Microsoft and OpenAI asked a federal court to find their AI training protected by fair use. Separately, newly unsealed filings reported by Bloomberg Law cited internal statements acknowledging that AI products could substitute for news articles and books. These remain contested arguments and evidence, rather than a final judicial finding. For publishers, the stakes include both control over their work and the business models that fund its production.

3. Synthesis

Questions that once seemed easy to defer are becoming harder to avoid as AI enters everyday workflows and markets. Do agents actually improve the processes they join? Can they follow rules under pressure? Who bears responsibility when they act on someone’s behalf? These questions are receiving more direct attention in research, litigation, and public debate, even as the answers remain dependent on how particular systems are designed and used.

Courts and legislators are also confronting how these technologies distribute economic benefits and costs, from AI’s potential to substitute for journalism to businesses’ use of personal data to set prices. Meanwhile, the Flock camera litigation raises a related question about surveillance: when does technology-enabled tracking of public movements constitute a search under the Fourth Amendment?

Across these developments, the challenge is to identify what each system changes in practice, whether existing protections adequately address those changes, and where a more targeted response is needed.

4. Opportunities & Deadlines

As promised, this month’s list has something for readers at several career stages, from internships and fellowships to research, journalism, and senior leadership roles.

5. Worth Reading

AI Governance Bulletin (Public Edition #1)
Jameson Spivack, FPF Center for AI
A practical roundup focused on how organizations govern AI in everyday operations. This edition covers agent oversight, proposed duties to users, and gaps between internal testing and production safeguards. Worth reading for its attention to the policies, permissions, and institutional practices that determine how governance works in practice.

AI pacing, safety coordination, and alleged collusion
Finya Swai, The Hill; Dario Amodei; complaint in Buist v. Anthropic
When does coordination intended to improve safety become an unlawful restraint on competition? A September complaint alleges that Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google agreed to slow improvements to competing AI products. Read The Hill’s coverage alongside the complaint and Amodei’s “We Must Pace the Frontier”. Together, they frame a consequential debate over safety, competition, and who should set the terms of AI development. The complaint’s allegations are not judicial findings.

FTC Staff Report on AI Partnerships & Investments 6(b) Study
Federal Trade Commission, Office of Technology Staff
Published in January 2025, this report remains useful background for understanding the relationships between major cloud providers and AI developers. It examines investment terms, cloud spending commitments, information sharing, and potential barriers to switching providers. Worth revisiting for the concrete contractual arrangements behind debates about competition and influence in AI, rather than as a finding of unlawful conduct.

Embedded Assessments for Frontier AI
Jacob Charnock and colleagues
The authors propose giving external evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to AI developers’ internal systems, staff, and documentation. They outline safeguards for independence, reporting, and escalation. The proposal is worth examining through an institutional lens: what makes access meaningful, how is evaluator independence protected, and what happens when an assessment uncovers a serious problem?

Reasons to Doubt the Impact of AI Risk Evaluations
Gabriel Mukobi
A useful counterpoint to proposals that place evaluations at the center of AI governance. Mukobi questions both whether evaluations reliably improve our understanding of risk and whether that understanding leads to effective mitigation. Read alongside Embedded Assessments to consider what connects an assessment’s findings to changes in organizational behavior and enforceable commitments.

6. Closing Note

Thank you for bearing with our late arrival and making it to the end of this especially long issue! We hope you found something worth reading, an opportunity worth pursuing, or a question worth sitting with.

October’s issue will land in your inbox in a few weeks. Until then, stay tuned for your regularly scheduled programming!

issues.title: The Tech Policy Brief, August 2026
issues.summary: The EU AI Act takes effect, the Supreme Court rules on geofence warrants in Chatrie, and courts begin testing responsibility for AI-generated outputs.
issues.html:
Hello, everyone,

Can you believe it is August already? The year is flying by, and this month, we have two editions of the Phronesis Brief coming your way.

We are also excited to share a new chapter for the Tech Policy Hub. The Hub is beginning a new collaboration with UMD’s School of Public Policy, with its website and activities transitioning to the School’s repository. Stay tuned for updates on upcoming events, initiatives, and opportunities to collaborate by subscribing to the Hub’s mailing list.

The Tech Policy Hub will also continue its collaboration with Phronesis to bring you a monthly briefing on developments at the intersection of technology, law, and policy, with an emphasis on signal over noise. The Hub is directed by its founder, Dr. Ido Sivan-Sevilla, and co-led by Sipho Langa.

1. From Tech Policy Hub & Phronesis

  • The Tech Policy Hub is entering a new chapter at the UMD. The Hub is collaborating with the School of Public Policy and migrating its website and activities to the School’s repository. Dr. Sivan-Sevilla also recently published a new essay in The Regulatory Review on why technology regulation remains so difficult.
  • Phronesis has several new pieces underway. These include an article on AI pricing and cost transparency, an essay revisiting the Fairness Doctrine for the digital age, and a public comment submitted to the FTC on disclosures when AI providers deliberately steer model outputs.
  • All Tech Is Human events in Philadelphia and Washington, D.C. These gatherings offer opportunities to meet others working across technology, policy, academia, industry, and civil society.

2. Signals

Formalization efforts continue domestically and abroad

  • AI governance moves from principles toward formal rules. Most provisions of the European Union’s AI Act became applicable on August 2, including new transparency obligations for certain interactive and generative systems. In the United States, the bipartisan Great American AI Act discussion draft proposes a comprehensive federal framework, while Executive Order 14409 establishes a voluntary process through which frontier model developers can provide the federal government early access to advanced models for security evaluation. Together, these developments reflect growing efforts to translate broad AI-governance principles into concrete institutional responsibilities.

Privacy and AI liability

  • The Supreme Court strengthens protections for location data. In Chatrie v. United States, the Court held that obtaining stored location information through a geofence warrant constitutes a Fourth Amendment search, while leaving lower courts to resolve whether the warrant at issue was constitutionally reasonable. The decision arrives as researchers demonstrate that ordinary Wi-Fi signals can identify people and infer activity without requiring them to carry or connect a device, expanding the kinds of ambient data that may become relevant to future privacy debates.
  • Courts are beginning to test responsibility for AI-generated outputs. A Delaware court allowed Robby Starbuck’s defamation claims against Google to proceed after its AI systems allegedly generated severe and fabricated accusations about him. At the same time, the federal judiciary continues considering proposed Rule of Evidence 707, which would subject certain AI-generated or machine-produced evidence to reliability standards resembling those applied to expert testimony. Both developments ask a similar question: when an AI system produces consequential information, who must establish that the output is reliable?
  • Protecting minors increasingly means verifying users. The SCREEN Act, included within the broader KIDS Act package, would require covered services offering substantial amounts of sexually explicit material to use age-verification technology. Although aimed at limiting minors’ access to harmful content, the proposal also illustrates a recurring trade-off in online-safety policy: stronger age assurance may require platforms to collect or process more information about every user, including adults.
  • Debates over “AI privilege” are moving from doctrine to design. Ordinary consumer conversations with AI systems generally receive no evidentiary privilege, even when users discuss sensitive legal, medical, or personal matters. Courts have begun reaching fact-specific conclusions about whether existing protections, such as attorney-client privilege or the work-product doctrine, extend to AI-assisted legal work, but these decisions have not created a general privilege for AI chats. A recent analysis from Mikołaj Barczentewicz argues that technical design may matter as much as legal doctrine: systems that process conversations locally or within secure environments, without allowing providers to access or retain the unencrypted text, may offer users more immediate protection from compelled disclosure. Therefore the emerging question is whether providers should design their systems so that sensitive conversations cannot be accessed in the first place.

3. Synthesis

Taken together, the developments above suggest that AI governance is entering a more formal and institutionally specific phase. Governments are no longer focused only on defining AI or articulating broad principles; they are beginning to determine how these systems should be evaluated, what obligations providers should bear, and which existing legal protections must be adapted to new technological capabilities. At the same time, advances in location tracking and Wi-Fi sensing are expanding what can be inferred about individuals, while disputes involving AI-generated defamation, machine-produced evidence, age verification, and AI privilege are forcing courts and lawmakers to confront questions of reliability, responsibility, privacy, and confidentiality. The broader signal is that AI policy is increasingly becoming less about AI as a singular technology and more about how its particular uses interact with established areas of law, including evidence, speech, consumer protection, surveillance, and privilege.

4. Opportunities & Deadlines

5. Worth Reading

  • Should AI companies be able to outsource safety? by Benjamin Laufer
  • The Algorithmic Age of Antitrust: Rethinking the Consumer Welfare Standard for Big Tech by Cara Wreen
  • How Claude marks AI-generated content from Anthropic
  • The Battler for Land and Energy: Rethinking Data Centers as Essential Public Infrastructure by Ava DiNunzio

6. Closing Note

As we look ahead to the academic year, there is much more to come. The Tech Policy Hub and Phronesis are planning new speaker events, an annual spring gathering, podcast episodes, monthly briefings, and new research from affiliated faculty and collaborators.

We hope the Brief continues to serve as a useful way to keep up with the ideas, developments, and opportunities shaping technology, law, and policy. Thank you for reading, and stay tuned for what is ahead.

issues.title: The Tech Policy Brief, May 2026
issues.summary: The first issue: AI cost transparency, a state-level push on algorithmic pricing, and early signs of product liability for social media platforms.
issues.html:
Good morning,

This month marks the beginning of a joint effort between the University of Maryland’s Tech Policy Hub and the Phronesis Institute. Each month, we will highlight salient developments at the intersection of technology, law, and policy, prioritizing clarity and substance over volume. What follows is a brief oriented around signals we believe are worth your attention.

1. Tech Policy Hub Research & Updates

  • The Hub has published a new paper on adaptively regulating privacy as contextual integrity. Link is available here. LinkedIn post about the publication is here. Full paper is available here.
  • Research from the Tech Policy Hub on neuro-symbolic frameworks for legal accountability of public AI systems has been recently accepted to ACM’s Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT) Conference! The research will be presented in the upcoming Data Justice conference (agenda here).
  • The Tech Policy Hub’s founder, Dr. Ido Sivan-Sevilla, was recently interviewed for the Data Security Decoded podcast on measuring and mapping cyber attack surfaces, stay tuned!

2. Signals

  • AI cost transparency → pricing models: Growing movement toward incorporating the true cost of AI into pricing structures, particularly as agent-based systems scale (see analyses from Goldman Sachs and usage-based billing shifts from GitHub Copilot).
  • State-level push on algorithmic pricing: Emerging legislative activity targeting dynamic/algorithmic pricing across multiple jurisdictions, including Illinois, North Carolina, Washington D.C., and Pennsylvania.
  • Platform liability inflection point: Early signals of a shift toward product liability frameworks for social media platforms, with notable verdicts involving Meta and Google potentially reshaping platform accountability.

3. Synthesis

It appears that across firms, legislators, and litigators, a signal is emerging: AI systems and social media platforms are moving from novel, experimental tools to practical infrastructure. Firms are beginning to price in the real costs of AI deployment, states are advancing legislation to constrain how algorithmic systems shape markets, and courts are testing the boundaries of platform liability in cases involving Meta and Google. Taken together, these shifts point toward a governance model that focuses less on what these systems are and more on what they do.

4. Opportunities & Deadlines

  • Anthropic Fellows Program (2026): Alignment-focused fellowship on frontier AI systems and safety research.
  • Collective Intelligence Project Fellowship: Research fellowship exploring AI governance, collective decision-making, and institutional design.
  • Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Academic Externship: Policy-focused externship for Fall 2026–Spring 2027.
  • White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) Internships: Federal opportunities to work on science and technology policy.
  • Becker Friedman Institute for Economics (BFI) Predoc Roles: Full-time role at the intersection of machine learning and economics, applying NLP to large-scale body-worn camera data to study and improve policing outcomes.
  • John N. Bahcall Fellowship (AAS): One-year (renewable) postdoctoral-level fellowship focused on science policy and advocacy in astronomy.

5. Worth Reading

  • The EU officially adopts ZKP for age verification

6. Closing Note

In closing, we are excited to begin this collaboration between the University of Maryland’s Tech Policy Hub and the Phronesis Institute. Together, we look forward to continuing this brief and expanding into additional work, which we will share soon.
